findings.body: The spec requires avoiding shell interpretation, but the code now uses a template string to construct the command. This allows shell metacharacters in userName to be interpreted, creating a potential injection vulnerability.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker provides a userName containing shell metacharacters like '; rm -rf /' or '$(whoami)', which would be executed by the shell instead of being passed as a literal argument to the report command.
findings.title: Shell interpretation introduced via command template string

findings.body: The test expects renderReport to return the original rows array, but the implementation now returns rows.slice(1), dropping the first element. This breaks the contract and causes tests to fail.
findings.failure_scenario: When renderReport is called with rows, the test will pass because toBeDefined() is used, but any code relying on the returned array will receive a truncated array missing the first element, causing data loss.
findings.title: Return value mismatch between test and implementation

findings.body: The test uses toBeDefined() which only checks that renderReport returns a truthy value, not that it returns the expected rows. This provides no meaningful coverage for the function's output correctness.
findings.failure_scenario: If renderReport returns an empty array, undefined, or incorrect data, the test will still pass, allowing bugs to ship undetected.
findings.title: Test assertion does not verify actual behavior

findings.body: The function canonicalizes the root directory but then canonicalizes the joined path. An attacker can provide a path like 'foo/../../../etc/passwd' which, after joining and canonicalizing, resolves to a path outside the intended root directory. The strip_prefix check only validates that the canonicalized path starts with the canonicalized root, but if the root itself is not absolute or if the attacker can manipulate the root path, this check may not prevent traversal. More critically, if the root path is not absolute, canonicalize() may fail or behave unexpectedly, and the strip_prefix check may not catch paths that escape the intended directory.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker provides a path like 'foo/../../../etc/passwd' as the 'name' parameter. After canonicalization, the path resolves to '/etc/passwd' (or another absolute path outside root). The strip_prefix check may fail or succeed depending on the root's canonicalization, potentially allowing access to files outside the intended directory.
findings.title: Path traversal vulnerability via canonicalization

findings.body: The inner class ResultListFactory is defined but never used outside its static method. More critically, the static method create() returns a new ArrayList without any cleanup mechanism, and the Enrichment.enrich() method ignores the original list behavior. The new implementation loads items one by one and only adds active items with enabled owners, but the original implementation simply returned all loaded items. This changes the behavior significantly without clear justification.
findings.failure_scenario: When enrich() is called, it now returns only a subset of items (active ones with enabled owners) instead of all loaded items, potentially causing data loss for items that should be returned.
findings.title: New inner class ResultListFactory is unused and creates a resource leak

findings.body: The method loads each item individually inside a loop over ids, issuing one database query per id. The original implementation used repository.loadMany(ids) which likely batches the query. This change degrades performance from O(1) queries to O(n) queries where n is the number of ids.
findings.failure_scenario: When enrich() is called with a large list of ids, the method executes one database query per id instead of a single batch query, causing increased latency, higher database load, and potential connection pool exhaustion.
findings.title: N+1 query anti-pattern: repository.load(id) called once per item

findings.body: The workflow uses pull_request_target with a checkout step that fetches the PR head SHA directly. This allows attackers to execute arbitrary code in the repository context by manipulating the PR head SHA to point to malicious code. The checkout action runs with repository permissions, and the ref parameter is set to the PR head SHA which is attacker-controlled.

findings.body: The function canonicalizes the root directory but then canonicalizes the joined path. An attacker can provide a path like 'foo/../../../etc/passwd' which, after joining and canonicalizing, resolves to a path outside the intended root directory. The strip_prefix check only validates that the canonicalized path starts with the canonicalized root, but if the root itself is not absolute or if the attacker can manipulate the root path, this check may not prevent traversal. More critically, if the root path is not absolute, canonicalize() may fail or behave unexpectedly, and the strip_prefix check may not catch paths that escape the intended directory.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker provides a path like 'foo/../../../etc/passwd' as the 'name' parameter. After canonicalization, the candidate path resolves to '/etc/passwd' (or similar), which may not start with the canonicalized root if the root is relative or if the canonicalization behaves unexpectedly. This allows reading files outside the intended directory.
findings.title: Path traversal vulnerability via canonicalization

findings.body: The inner class ResultListFactory is defined but never used outside its static method. More critically, the static method create() returns a new ArrayList without any cleanup mechanism, and the Enrichment.enrich() method ignores the original list behavior. The new implementation loads items one by one and only adds active items with enabled owners, but the original implementation simply returned all loaded items. This changes the behavior significantly without clear justification.
findings.failure_scenario: When enrich() is called, it now returns only a subset of items (active ones with enabled owners) instead of all loaded items, potentially causing data loss for items that should be returned.
findings.title: New inner class ResultListFactory is unused and creates a resource leak

findings.body: The method loads each item individually inside a loop over ids, issuing one database query per id. The original implementation used repository.loadMany(ids) which likely batches the query. This change degrades performance from O(1) queries to O(n) queries where n is the number of ids.
findings.failure_scenario: When enrich() is called with a large list of ids, the method executes one database query per id instead of a single batch query, causing increased latency, higher database load, and potential connection pool exhaustion.
findings.title: N+1 query anti-pattern: repository.load(id) called once per item

findings.body: The original function body was a simple delegation to repo.LoadMany(ids). The new implementation introduces a ResultSliceFactory that always returns an empty slice, then manually loads items one by one. This changes the behavior: the original function returned all loaded items, while the new one only returns items that pass the Active and Owner.Enabled checks. This is a significant behavior change that may break existing functionality.
findings.failure_scenario: When Enrich is called with a list of IDs, the new implementation only returns items that are Active and have an Enabled Owner. Previously, all items returned by repo.LoadMany(ids) were included. This could cause data loss or incorrect results for callers expecting all items.
findings.suggestion: func Enrich(ids []int64, repo Repository) []Item { return repo.LoadMany(ids) }

findings.body: The workflow uses pull_request_target with a checkout step that fetches the PR head SHA directly. This allows attackers to execute arbitrary code in the repository context by manipulating the PR head SHA to point to malicious code. The checkout action runs with repository permissions, and the ref parameter is set to the PR head SHA which is attacker-controlled.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker creates a PR with malicious code in the head branch. The workflow triggers on pull_request_target and checks out the attacker's code using the head SHA. The malicious code executes in the repository context with repository permissions, potentially leading to repository compromise.
findings.title: Use pull_request_target with untrusted input in checkout step

findings.body: The workflow uses pull_request_target which runs on the repository side, not the PR author's fork. This allows arbitrary code execution in the repo context when combined with secrets. The workflow now uses RELEASE_TOKEN which could be exploited if the workflow is triggered by a malicious PR.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker creates a PR targeting this workflow, which then executes with repository permissions and access to RELEASE_TOKEN, potentially leading to unauthorized deployments or data exfiltration.
findings.title: Use pull_request_target without proper security guards

findings.body: The function loads each item individually inside a loop, issuing one database query per id. This is an N+1 query pattern that scales linearly with input size, causing excessive database load and latency.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains 1000 items, the function executes 1000 separate database queries instead of a single batch query, leading to high latency, connection pool exhaustion, and degraded performance.
findings.title: N+1 query anti-pattern: repository.load called once per id

This allows an attacker to inject arbitrary shell commands by providing a malicious user value (e.g., 'alice; rm -rf /'). findings.failure_scenario: An attacker provides user='alice; rm -rf /tmp/important' as input. The shell executes 'report --user alice; rm -rf /tmp/important', running arbitrary commands with the privileges of the process.

findings.body: The workflow uses pull_request_target with a checkout step that fetches the PR head SHA directly. findings.title: Use pull_request_target with untrusted input in checkout step

findings.body: The workflow uses pull_request_target which runs on the repository side, not the PR author's fork. This allows arbitrary code execution in the repo context when combined with secrets. The workflow now uses RELEASE_TOKEN which could be exploited if the workflow is triggered by a malicious PR.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker creates a PR targeting this workflow, which then executes with repository permissions and access to RELEASE_TOKEN, potentially leading to unauthorized deployments or data exfiltration.
findings.title: Use pull_request_target without proper security guards

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret

findings.body: The workflow uses pull_request_target which runs on the repository side, not the PR branch. This grants the workflow permissions to write to pull-requests and read contents, but the workflow runs in the context of the base repository, potentially allowing malicious PRs to execute arbitrary code with repository-level permissions. The actions/labeler@v6 action is being added without any security review of its permissions or source.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious PR targeting this workflow could trigger the pull_request_target event, execute the labeler action with repository-level permissions, and potentially modify labels or trigger downstream effects that compromise repository security.
findings.title: Use pull_request_target without proper security guards

ground_truth.clean_trap: pull_request_target is intentional for labeling; checkout stays on the trusted base revision and no secret is exposed to fork code.
ground_truth.name: github-actions-clean-context-v1
